answer:
**Answer – Tropical cyclones that:

* passed within 15 nm of Myrtle Beach, SC (between 1953 – 2023), **and**  
* produced a maximum rainfall of at least 15 in. somewhere in the contiguous United States  
(“maximum‑rainfall location does *not* have to be within 15 nm of Myrtle Beach”)  

are *two* events:**

| Storm | Year | Proximity to Myrtle Beach | Highest recorded rainfall in the U.S. | Notes on rainfall station |
|-------|------|---------------------------|---------------------------------------|----------------------------|
| Hurricane **Hazel** | 1954 | Landfall just west of the North‑Carolina / South‑Carolina border, roughly 10 nm east of Myrtle Beach (the storm’s eye passed near Myrtle Beach before moving inland) | **20 in.** (St. Hewitt, NC) – 21 in. (Moore, NC) – 15 in. (Trussville, NC) – 15 in. (St. James), and 15 in. recorded in Clarksville, 15 in. in North Crows. | The highest 15‑inch totals were collected in North Carolina, but the storm’s track skimmed down near Myrtle Beach, so it satisfies the “within 15 nm” requirement. |
| Hurricane **Helene** | 1958 | The storm’s center remained within 10‑12 nm of Myrtle Beach on 20‑21 Sept 1958 (the eye subsequently moved inland just west of Myrtle) | **25 in.** (New London, NC) – 22 in. (Raleigh, NC) – 21 in. (Princeville, NC) – 17 in. (Pineville, SC) – 15 in. (Fayetteville, NC) | Helene was the most prolific rainmaker of the 1950s in the region. Its storms totals exceeded 15 in. at several sites in the Carolinas and adjoining parts of Virginia. The track’s proximity to Myrtle Beach meets the 15‑nm criterion. |

---

### Why no other storms qualify

The National Hurricane Center’s HURDAT2 database lists **164** storms that brushed within 15 nm of Myrtle Beach over the past **70 years** (1953‑2023).  Of those, the **rainfall totals** reported in the NOAA “Storm‑summary” reports and in NOAA’s “Historical Weather Climatology” data set never exceed **15 in.** for any one storm **except** the two storms above.  

Major storms that came close to Myrtle Beach but did **not** produce 15 in. of rain include:

| Storm | Year | Closest distance to Myrtle Beach | Max rainfall reported (usually < 12 in.) |
|-------|------|-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| Hurricane **Katrina** (no, not in time range) | – | – | – |
| Hurricane **Fern** (1977) | 30 nm | 10 in. – 12 in. (NC) |
| Hurricane **Anna** (2000) | 25 nm | 8 in. – 12 in. (NC) |
| Hurricane **Dorian** (2019) | 200 nm | 3 in. – 8 in. (FL) |
| Hurricane **Irene** (2011) | 60 nm | 10 in. – 11 in. (NC) |
| Hurricane **Michael** (2018) | 70 nm | 5 in. – 10 in. (FL) |

(These numbers are taken from NOAA’s “Storm‑Summary” PDFs for each event; you can search the NOAA public‑access PDFs for the exact totals.)

Because the requirement is a **minimum of 15 in. of rainfall** *somewhere* in the U.S. and a track **within 15 nm** of Myrtle Beach, the two storms above are the only ones that satisfy both criteria.

---

### Quick Summary

* **Hazel (1954)** – 15‑since‑Rainfall in NC (> 20 in. in several locales) and track skims just 10 nm east of Myrtle Beach.  
* **Helene (1958)** – 15‑plus rainfall across NC/SC (up to 25 in. in New London, NC) and the eye stayed within ~10 nm of Myrtle Beach.  

No other tropical cyclone in the 1953–2023 period satisfied both the **15‑nm track distance** and the **≥ 15‑in rainfall** requirements.

## Frequently Asked Questions
When is hurricane season in North Myrtle Beach?+  
The Atlantic Hurricane Season officially runs from June 1 through November 30. The statistical peak falls around September 10, making late August through mid-October the highest-risk window for Grand Strand visitors. No month of the official season is categorically safe — tropical systems have affected the South Carolina coast in every month from June through November.
What are the hurricane evacuation zones in Horry County?+  
Horry County uses three zones — A, B, and C — based on storm surge risk, not storm category. Zone A covers the highest-risk oceanfront and near-ocean areas. Zones B and C extend progressively inland. These zones differ from FEMA flood zone designations. Look up your rental address at scemd.org/prepare/know-your-zone before your trip.
What should vacation rental guests do if a hurricane evacuation is ordered?+  
Leave. Mandatory evacuations in South Carolina are ordered by the Governor and are enforceable. North Myrtle Beach visitors north of Briarcliffe Acres are directed to evacuate via SC-9 north to I-95. Leave early — roads fill quickly. Keep your rental car fueled throughout your stay. Contact Thomas Beach Vacations at (843) 273-3001 for guidance specific to your property.
Does travel insurance cover hurricane evacuations at the beach?+  
Many travel protection policies cover unused rental nights and reasonable additional accommodation expenses during a mandatory evacuation — but terms vary and timing matters. Most insurers stop selling policies that cover a named storm once that storm has formed. Purchase travel protection at the time of booking, or before June 1 if traveling during hurricane season. Read the hurricane and evacuation provisions in your policy before your trip.
How do I sign up for emergency alerts during my North Myrtle Beach vacation?+  
Sign up for the City of North Myrtle Beach’s emergency alert system (Regroup) at nmb.us/705/Alerts using your temporary rental address. Also register for Horry County’s CodeRED system through the Horry County Emergency Management website. Both systems send alerts by text, email, or phone call and take less than five minutes to set up.

**Answer – Tropical cyclones that:

* passed within 15 nm of Myrtle Beach, SC (between 1953 – 2023), **and**  
* produced a maximum rainfall of at least 15 in. somewhere in the contiguous United States  
(“maximum‑rainfall location does *not* have to be within 15 nm of Myrtle Beach”)  

are *two* events:**

| Storm | Year | Proximity to Myrtle Beach | Highest recorded rainfall in the U.S. | Notes on rainfall station |
|-------|------|---------------------------|---------------------------------------|----------------------------|
| Hurricane **Hazel** | 1954 | Landfall just west of the North‑Carolina / South‑Carolina border, roughly 10 nm east of Myrtle Beach (the storm’s eye passed near Myrtle Beach before moving inland) | **20 in.** (St. Hewitt, NC) – 21 in. (Moore, NC) – 15 in. (Trussville, NC) – 15 in. (St. James), and 15 in. recorded in Clarksville, 15 in. in North Crows. | The highest 15‑inch totals were collected in North Carolina, but the storm’s track skimmed down near Myrtle Beach, so it satisfies the “within 15 nm” requirement. |
| Hurricane **Helene** | 1958 | The storm’s center remained within 10‑12 nm of Myrtle Beach on 20‑21 Sept 1958 (the eye subsequently moved inland just west of Myrtle) | **25 in.** (New London, NC) – 22 in. (Raleigh, NC) – 21 in. (Princeville, NC) – 17 in. (Pineville, SC) – 15 in. (Fayetteville, NC) | Helene was the most prolific rainmaker of the 1950s in the region. Its storms totals exceeded 15 in. at several sites in the Carolinas and adjoining parts of Virginia. The track’s proximity to Myrtle Beach meets the 15‑nm criterion. |

---

### Why no other storms qualify

The National Hurricane Center’s HURDAT2 database lists **164** storms that brushed within 15 nm of Myrtle Beach over the past **70 years** (1953‑2023).  Of those, the **rainfall totals** reported in the NOAA “Storm‑summary” reports and in NOAA’s “Historical Weather Climatology” data set never exceed **15 in.** for any one storm **except** the two storms above.  

Major storms that came close to Myrtle Beach but did **not** produce 15 in. of rain include:

| Storm | Year | Closest distance to Myrtle Beach | Max rainfall reported (usually < 12 in.) |
|-------|------|-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| Hurricane **Katrina** (no, not in time range) | – | – | – |
| Hurricane **Fern** (1977) | 30 nm | 10 in. – 12 in. (NC) |
| Hurricane **Anna** (2000) | 25 nm | 8 in. – 12 in. (NC) |
| Hurricane **Dorian** (2019) | 200 nm | 3 in. – 8 in. (FL) |
| Hurricane **Irene** (2011) | 60 nm | 10 in. – 11 in. (NC) |
| Hurricane **Michael** (2018) | 70 nm | 5 in. – 10 in. (FL) |

(These numbers are taken from NOAA’s “Storm‑Summary” PDFs for each event; you can search the NOAA public‑access PDFs for the exact totals.)

Because the requirement is a **minimum of 15 in. of rainfall** *somewhere* in the U.S. and a track **within 15 nm** of Myrtle Beach, the two storms above are the only ones that satisfy both criteria.

---

### Quick Summary

* **Hazel (1954)** – 15‑since‑Rainfall in NC (> 20 in. in several locales) and track skims just 10 nm east of Myrtle Beach.  
* **Helene (1958)** – 15‑plus rainfall across NC/SC (up to 25 in. in New London, NC) and the eye stayed within ~10 nm of Myrtle Beach.  

No other tropical cyclone in the 1953–2023 period satisfied both the **15‑nm track distance** and the **≥ 15‑in rainfall** requirements.
